    Mwni

    -

    Thank you for this proposal and the additional work composing together a preview of the existing standards. I propose to unify the file directives:

    • localization.primary_uri
    • localization.secondary_uris
    • properties.primary_display.primary_uri
    • properties.primary_display.secondary_uris
    • properties.files
    • properties.expiration.files

    as all of these serve the same purpose with some conditions/modifications. It hence makes sense to define one universal data structure with modifiers such as disposition or animated, like this:

    {
    "type": "generative_art",
    "name": "XR-ART 1234",
    "description": "..."
    "files": [
        {
            "mime": "image/png",
            "uri": "ipfs://QmABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ123456789101112",
            "disposition": "original",
            "encryption": "AES-128"
        },
        {
            "mime": "image/png",
            "uri": "https://bucket-name.s3.Region.amazonaws.com/XR-ART1234.png",
            "disposition": "original",
            "encryption": "AES-128",
            "mirror": true
        },
        {
            "mime": "image/png",
            "uri": "ipfs://HIJKLMNOPQmABCDEFGQRST56789101112UVWXYZ1234",
            "disposition": "display",
        },
        {
            "mime": "video/mp4",
            "uri": "ipfs://EFGQNOV101112URSWXYZ129T567HPQmABCD8IJKLM34",
            "disposition": "display",
            "animated": true
        },
        {
            "mime": "image/png",
            "uri": "https://xr-art.com/nfts/expired.png",
            "disposition": "expiration"
        },
    ],
    ...
}

    I think that unifying the files into the root definitely simplifies the structure and makes a lot of sense.
    Rather than embedding the disposition into the file object itself, I propose to convert the "files" field from an array to an object with the disposition acting as the field to prevent repetition. The community can then define a set of expected file field based on the "type" of the NFT.

    {
   "type":"generative_art",
    "name":"XR-ART 1234",
    "description": "A masterpiece powered by code.",
     ...
    "files":{
        "display":[
            {
                "mime":"image/png",
                "uri":"ipfs://QmABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ55555555555555",
            },

                "mirror":true
            }, 
        ],
        "localized":[
             ...
        ],

        ]

    Mwni Feb 17, 2022

    Using the flat structure, one could quite trivially program a "ranking" algorithm that is very tolerant. Let's say you want to present the animated thumbnail of a NFT. The ranking algorithm could then give files with the disposition 'display' +10 points, if the 'animated' field is set, give another 10 points. If it's a mirror, subtract 1 point, etc. Even if there is no exact match, you could still retrieve the most optimal file.

    With the addition of the alterations to your recommendations described in this comment, I expect localization to be handled as such:

    {
    "type":"generative_art",
    ...
    "description": "This is true art"
    ...
    "localization":{
        "default": "en",
        "locales":["en","dn","fr"],
    },
    "files":{
        "display":[
           ...
        ],
        "localized":[
                {
                    "uri":"ipfs://QmABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ123456789101112/{locale}.json"
                },
                {
                    "uri":"https://bucket-name.s3.Region.amazonaws.com/{tokenID}/{locale}.json",
                    "mirror":true
                },
        ],
       "expired":[
            ...
        ]
    },
   ...

}

    Rather than returning an entire copy of the metadata file with just a few fields that were localized, I propose to only return the fields that were localized to prevent repetition and optimize size.

    In your example of the German metadata file:

    • https://metadata.xr-art.com/nft/000B013A95F14B0E44F78A264E41/de
    {
   "description": "Das ist wahre Kunst"
}

    x-Tokenize Feb 18, 2022
    Author

    -

    The flow envisioned with this approach works like this:

    1. The application loads an NFT with the default localization as defined by the creator.
    2. User would then interact with the NFT within the application to translate fields to a localized version if one is provided and so desired.
    3. If the user interacts to translate, via dropdown or if set in a global application setting (i.e. translate to "dn" if available) :
      3a. Make a secondary request to pull localized data and modify the original object on the application side with the localized data.

    The rationale here is that if there are localization options for the NFT then the application will still have to make a second request regardless to pull the requested localized data which can then just be used to alter the localized fields. A few localization options would result in a just a few KB but, at scale repeating the data 155 times for all possible localization options would be a huge waste if repeating the entire file.

    Perhaps an even better improvement would be to add all localization options to a singular file like this:

    • https://metadata.xr-art.com/nft/000B013A95F14B0E44F78A264E41/localizedFields.json
    {
   "description":{
     "dn":"Das ist wahre Kunst",
     "fr":"C'est de l'art véritable",
     "pl":"To jest prawdziwa sztuka",
      ...
      }
}

    This approach would allow for many localizations to be handled in the same file which significantly increases scalability, decreases storage requirements and minimizes the number of files that need to be tracked.

    A disadvantage to this approach would be an increased probability of application error for deeply nested localized fields. One way to mitigate this risk would be to provide localization directly in the original metadata but, could result in bloated and useless data.

    Here is the standard I use in my dapps for saving/loading/parsing IPFS data that's NOT NFTs.

    CLXS-004

    The only addition I would suggest to the XLS-24d standard is the/a domain.

    "domain": {
    "name": "swordfish.io",
    "version": "0.0.1"
 },

    You already excluded external_url in your standard above and that IMO is a must.

    This would be an upgrade but I honestly wouldn't upload an NFT to XRPL mainnet you couldn't change without the base fields from the well established companies (Open Sea, Solana, BSC). It could at any moment change and the interoperability would be missed.*

    BASE:

    name
description
external_url
image: 'ipfs://'
attributes

    Notice how Solana duplicated the image and the files. I would also do this to ensure interoperability if you use the display field referenced above.

    *They could add XRP or a side chain could be created to connect the two.

  "required": [
    "schema",
    "type",
    "name",
    "description",
    "image",
    
  ],
  "properties": {
    "schema": {
      "type": "string""format": "uri"
    },
    "nftType": {
      "type": "string",
      "pattern":(^[a-zA-Z]+\.v[0-9]+$)
    },
    "name": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "description": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "image": {
      "type": "string",
      "contentMediaType": "image/png",
      "format": "uri"
    },
    "animation_url": {
      "type": "string",
      "contentMediaType": "video/mp4",
      "format": "uri"
    },
    "video": {
      "type": "string",
      "contentMediaType": "video/mp4",
      "format": "uri"
    },
    "audio": {
      "type": "string",
      "contentMediaType": "audio/mpeg",
      "format": "uri"
    },
    "file": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "uri"
    },
    "collection": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name": {
          "type": "string"
        },
        "family": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "name"
      ]
    },
    "attributes": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "name": {
            "type": "string"
          },
          "description": {
            "type": "string"
          }"value": {
            "type": [
              "string",
              "int",
              "float"
            ]
          }
        },
        "required": [
          "name",
          "value"
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}

    An example

    {
   "schema":"https://nftmaster.com/nftmaster.v0Schema",
   "nftType":"nftmaster.v0",
   "name":"NFTMASTER NFT",

   "image":"ipfs://bafkreics7w2f724qc2pfrcbrrkfmwzruho5m4nzkg75kfilju2cp3e3cxa",
   "video":null,
   "animation":null,
   "audio":null,
   "file":null,
   "external_link":"https://nftmaster.com",
   "collection":{
      "name":"Andrews collection",
      "family":""
   },
   "attributes":[
      {
         "name":"Background",
         "value":"Blue",
         "description":null
      }
   ]
}

    ajkagy
    Aug 31, 2022

    -

    since XLS20 seems to be only 2 weeks away from implementation onto main net I want to stoke conversation on this again.

    XLS24 gives a lot of flexibility for future use cases beyond just art, but the immediate implications and use case in the next few months will be 95% art based NFTs. Thinking in broader terms of not just on the XRPL, but across the whole industry, projects should be cognizant of implementing a minimum standards (similar to the opensea standard) of sorts for easy implementation and compatibility. Many of the large EVM based chains have very similar metadata standards with small deviations/differences.

    The Base Art NFT example above seems to fill that minimum standard.

    A thought on adding collection attributes. on EVM chains collections are mutable user defined within marketplaces. NFTs are grouped based on the contract they were minted from, but users can add new NFTs from other sources into a collection. There are both pros and cons to adding collection attributes into the metadata itself.

    I do believe we are just scratching the surface here with the application of NFTs on the XRPL. Like you have mentioned, most projects that are anticipating the amendment are art based and will be requiring a rather simple schema to get their projects out there. The base art example should be sufficient and is similar enough to other existing standards that marketplaces and consuming applications shouldn't have an issue parsing multiple schemas to create a visualization of the metadata.

    Things will need to be more uniform when we are defining other NFT types like ticketing, digital identity, music, access control systems.
    Most likely these other nftTypes will also contain similar fields described in the base art example therefore enabling them to be consumed by marketplaces and gallery applications; As an nftType becomes more popular, those applications will also adopt those schemas to visualize the additional information if it fits in their business model!

    On the topic of the collection attribute, I thought it was good as an identifier for consuming applications to easily identify a project defined collection. Thinking further into it, this can also be handled in other ways such as using a combination of the taxon and issuer address.

    The metadata file should have both IPFS CIDv1 and CIDv0 like this image.
    IPFS gives you for the NFT the CIDv0 but then what appears in the explorers is CIDv1. So there is always uncertainty about the true correspondence between the CIDv0 and the corresponding CIDv1. It exists the tool (CID inspector) that converts one to the other, but that information should be in the metadata file in order to anyone check the correspondence directly just opening the metadata file, not having to go to the CID inspector to make sure there is correspondence.

    (To check in Bithomp: https://bithomp.com/explorer/rMGqQpJnjZhd64uzGzq7Zm1AZG7iD7NTu1
